## Overview

This reading prepares you for the DataLab session. It explains the cognitive tasks you'll complete and why we're collecting these data.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Data Dictionary
For a complete reference of all variables collected, see the [Data Dictionary](data-dictionary.qmd).
:::

## What You'll Be Measuring

DataLab includes six stations measuring different aspects of human cognition and behaviour. Here's the background on each:

### Station 1: Reaction Time (Reflex Test)

![](images/station1-reflex.png){.station-card}

{{< term reaction_time "Reaction time" >}} is the interval between a stimulus and your response to it. In the ruler-drop task, we measure **simple reaction time** — how quickly you can respond to a single, expected stimulus.

The physics is elegant: when you catch a falling ruler, the distance it fell before you caught it tells us how long your reaction took. Using the equation for free-falling objects (d = ½gt²), we can convert centimetres into milliseconds.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why It Matters
Reaction time is one of the most reliable measures in psychology. Your data will show how consistent (or variable) human performance is, even on simple tasks. We can also look for practice effects — do you get faster across trials?
:::

### Station 2: Memory (Mind Palace)

![](images/station2-mind-palace.png){.station-card}

The memory task measures {{< term working_memory >}} — how many items you can hold in mind while performing another task.

Miller (1956) famously proposed that we can hold about **7 ± 2** items in short-term memory — the "magical number seven." But the distraction task (maths problems) interferes with rehearsal, so performance typically drops.

We'll also examine the **serial position effect**: people tend to remember words from the beginning of a list (primacy) and end of a list (recency) better than the middle. Your position-by-position recall data will let us test this pattern.

### Station 3: Time and Magnitude Perception (Time Warp)

![](images/station3-time-warp.png){.station-card}

How accurately do we perceive time? Research shows that our internal clocks are surprisingly inaccurate and can be influenced by many factors.

This station measures three types of estimation:

1. **Time estimation** — How accurately can you judge 60 seconds?
2. **Visual magnitude estimation** — How accurately can you judge line lengths by looking?
3. **Tactile magnitude estimation** — How accurately can you judge lengths by touch alone?

::: {.callout-tip}
## Cross-Modal Comparison
By comparing visual and tactile estimation, we can explore whether some senses are more accurate than others for judging physical properties.
:::

### Station 4: Psychic Staring (Sixth Sense)

![](images/station4-sixth-sense.png){.station-card}

Can humans detect when they're being watched? This is a testable empirical question!

The staring detection task uses {{< term signal_detection "signal detection theory" >}}:

- **Hits**: Correctly detecting when someone IS staring
- **False alarms**: Saying "staring" when they're NOT
- **Misses**: Saying "not staring" when they ARE
- **Correct rejections**: Correctly detecting when they're NOT staring

If people cannot actually detect staring, we'd expect performance to be at **chance level** (about 50% correct, or 3 out of 6 trials).

### Station 5: Randomness (Lady Luck)

![](images/station5-lady-luck.png){.station-card}

Humans are notoriously bad at generating random sequences. When asked to produce "random" numbers, people:

- Avoid repeating the same number twice in a row (even though true randomness includes repetitions)
- Avoid patterns (even though random sequences often contain streaks)
- Favour certain numbers (often 7!)

This station also includes dice rolling and coin flipping, which let us compare **true** random outcomes (from dice/coins) with **human-generated** random sequences.

::: {.callout-note}
## The Gambler's Fallacy
Many people believe that after a streak of heads, tails is "due." This is false — each flip is independent. Your data will likely show longer runs than most people expect!
:::

### Station 6: Metacognition (Frontal Lob)

![](images/station6-frontal-lob.png){.station-card}

{{< term metacognition "Metacognition" >}} is thinking about your own thinking — including how well you know your own abilities.

The throwing task measures {{< term calibration >}}: the match between your self-assessed ability and your actual performance.

- **Overconfidence**: Rating yourself higher than your performance
- **Underconfidence**: Rating yourself lower than your performance
- **Well-calibrated**: Your rating matches your performance

Research consistently shows that people are poorly calibrated — often overconfident about easy tasks and underconfident about hard ones.

## The Pre-Post Design

DataLab uses a **within-subjects** design to measure mood change. You'll rate your mood, energy, and stress both **before** and **after** the stations.

This design is powerful because each person serves as their own control. By comparing your "before" to your "after," we eliminate individual differences — we're measuring change within you, not differences between people.

::: {.callout-important}
## Teaching Application
When we learn about paired t-tests, we'll analyse whether DataLab systematically affected mood, energy, or stress. Did participation make people feel better? Worse? More or less stressed?
:::

## Why Generate Our Own Data?

### Learning with Real Data

When we analyse data you've generated:

- You understand what the numbers represent
- You can connect statistics to real experiences
- The results are genuinely unknown (not textbook examples)

### Experiencing Both Roles

Acting as both **participant** and **tester** teaches you:

- The importance of standardised procedures
- How instructions affect behaviour
- Why research protocols exist

## Preparing for the Lab

### Before You Arrive

1. **Watch the preview video** — Module introduction (5 minutes)
2. **Read this page** — Understand what you'll be doing
3. **Check your lab allocation** — Lab A or Lab B

### What to Bring

- Your phone or laptop (for Qualtrics data entry)
- A pen (backup for paper recording)

### What to Expect

| Time | Activity |
|------|----------|
| 0:00-0:15 | Welcome, Part 1 survey, form groups |
| 0:15-1:45 | Rotate through 6 stations (~12-15 min each) |
| 1:45-1:55 | Part 2 survey |
| 1:55-2:00 | Debrief & wrap-up |

## Working in Pairs

At each station, you'll work with a partner:

1. One person is the **participant** (completes the task)
2. One person is the **tester** (administers the task, records data)
3. Then you **swap roles**

This means everyone experiences both perspectives.

## Group Formation

By the end of the lab, you should have formed your **project group** (3-4 students).

Consider:

- Can you meet regularly outside class?
- Do you have complementary strengths?
- Will you be reliable partners?

You'll work together all term on the group research project.
